claim: sp7:EGFP expression was first detected in clusters of cells in the skin, immediately followed by detection of calcified matrix.
source: Weak sp7:EGFP expression was first detected in clusters of cells in the skin, immediately followed by detection of calcified matrix (Figure 1A d1–d2 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by direct observation in live imaging experiments shown in Figure 1A and supplementary figures, representing experimental data.

claim: The distribution of calcified matrix correlated with the distribution of sp7:EGFP+ cells throughout scale development.
source: Throughout subsequent scale development, the distribution of calcified matrix correlated with the distribution of sp7:EGFP+ cells (Figure 1A, d2–d6; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This claim is supported by time-series imaging data showing co-localization of sp7:EGFP and calcified matrix.

claim: sp7:EGFP labels the dermal cell population that deposits calcified extracellular matrix comprising the scale plate.
source: Throughout subsequent scale development, the distribution of calcified matrix correlated with the distribution of sp7:EGFP+ cells (Figure 1A, d2–d6; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) suggesting that sp7:EGFP labeled the dermal cell population that deposits calcified extracellular matrix comprising the scale plate.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between sp7:EGFP expression and calcified matrix distribution observed in the data.

claim: Early sp7:EGFP+ dSFC clusters that lacked detectable calcified matrix showed a bi-layer papilla corresponding with structures described in histological and ultrastructural studies.
source: Early sp7:EGFP+ dSFC clusters that lacked detectable calcified matrix showed a bi-layer papilla corresponding with structures described in histological and ultrastructural studies (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) and comparison with previous histological studies.

claim: sp7:EGFP labels developing scales from very early in morphogenesis and likely earlier than other scale osteoblast markers.
source: Therefore, sp7:EGFP labels developing scales from very early in morphogenesis and likely earlier than other scale osteoblast markers (Iwasaki et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is based on the timing of sp7:EGFP expression observed in the data and comparison with other markers cited in the literature.

claim: Scales grew centripetally from the scale focus with a posterior bias leading to polarized extension through the addition of dSFCs and calcified matrix.
source: Following their initial appearance, scales grew centripetally from the scale focus with a posterior bias leading to polarized extension through the addition of dSFCs and calcified matrix (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequential labeling experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: In fully formed scales, sp7:EGFP+ dSFCs were arranged in a monolayer along the deep aspect of the calcified matrix but also looped around to cover the superficial surface.
source: In fully formed scales, sp7:EGFP+ dSFCs were arranged in a monolayer along the deep aspect of the calcified matrix but also looped around to cover the superficial surface, overlapping with the intensely ARS-labeled limiting layer (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data showing the spatial arrangement of dSFCs in mature scales.

claim: Scale primordia are added sequentially across the skin during development in zebrafish.
source: In-toto repeated live imaging of individual zebrafish revealed similar sequential addition of scale primordia (Figure 1B–1F, Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by live imaging data showing the temporal sequence of scale appearance.

claim: The first scales were found in a row on the caudal peduncle followed by a second row that formed on the flank above the ribs.
source: The first scales were found in a row on the caudal peduncle followed by a second row that formed on the flank above the ribs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data showing the initial sites of scale formation.

claim: Within one day, two complete rows of scales formed.
source: Within one day, two complete rows of scales formed (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data.

claim: Additional rows were added dorsally and ventrally, and columns were added anteriorly and posteriorly.
source: Additional rows were added dorsally and ventrally, and columns were added anteriorly and posteriorly (Figure 1B–1D; Figure 1—figure supplement 2F–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequential imaging data showing the pattern of scale addition.

claim: A third scale origin appeared just posterior to the mandible and spread along the ventral surface to meet the ventral row scales just posterior to the pectoral fin insertion.
source: Finally, a third scale origin appeared just posterior to the mandible and spread along the ventral surface to meet the ventral row scales just posterior to the pectoral fin insertion (Figure 1E; Figure 1—figure supplement 2J).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data showing the ventral scale formation pattern.

claim: The complete squamation process took approximately 13 days under optimized conditions.
source: Under optimized conditions, this process took ~13 days (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by longitudinal measurements of individual fish during squamation.

claim: The complete coat of scales is arranged in a half-offset, hexagonal grid on the juvenile fish.
source: These events lead to a complete coat of scales arranged in a half-offset, hexagonal grid on the juvenile fish (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data showing the final scale pattern.

claim: Sequential addition of skin appendage primordia, leading to a tightly packed hexagonal grid, is a feature of epidermal appendage development common to both amniotes and anamniote fishes.
source: Our observations of scale development indicate that sequential addition of skin appendage primordia, leading to a tightly packed hexagonal grid, is a feature of epidermal appendage development common to both amniotes and anamniote fishes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed pattern in zebrafish and comparison with known patterns in amniotes.

claim: Wnt/β-catenin signaling is necessary for scale development.
source: To inhibit Wnt/β-catenin signaling during scale development, we used the hs:dkk1 transgenic line that allows conditional expression of a potent and selective Wnt/β-catenin signaling inhibitor (Glinka et al., 1998; Stoick-Cooper et al., 2007). As predicted, inhibiting Wnt/β-catenin beginning prior to the appearance of sp7:EGFP+ papillae prevented scale formation (Figure 2A and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental manipulation using hs:dkk1 transgenic line and observation of scale formation phenotype.

claim: Early Dkk1 treatment blocked localized expression of the Wnt/β-catenin signaling activity reporter 7xTCF:mCherry.
source: This early treatment also blocked localized expression of the Wnt/β-catenin signaling activity reporter 7xTCF:mCherry (Figure 2B) (Moro et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data showing loss of reporter expression after Dkk1 treatment.

claim: Wnt/β-catenin inhibition prevented fin outgrowth and formation of pelvic fin rays.
source: Beyond scale phenotypes, Wnt/β-catenin inhibition prevented fin outgrowth and formation of pelvic fin rays (Figure 2A and D)
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and measurement data from Dkk1-treated fish.

claim: Wnt/β-catenin signaling has a role in fin development, in addition to previously documented functions in fin regeneration.
source: Beyond scale phenotypes, Wnt/β-catenin inhibition prevented fin outgrowth and formation of pelvic fin rays (Figure 2A and D), demonstrating a role for this pathway in fin development, in addition to previously documented functions in fin regeneration (Kawakami et al., 2006; Stoick-Cooper et al., 2007; Wehner et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and comparison with previous studies on fin regeneration.

claim: Scale and fin phenotypes from Wnt inhibition were not caused by a generalized retardation of development.
source: Scale and fin phenotypes were not caused by a generalized retardation of development, as Dkk1-overexpressing fish achieved sizes similar to those of non-transgenic, heat-shocked sibling controls (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurement data showing similar body sizes between treated and control fish.

claim: Wnt/β-catenin signaling activity was evident before sp7:EGFP+ scale papilla had formed.
source: Live imaging of fish doubly transgenic for 7xTCF:mCherry and sp7:EGFP showed that, as predicted, Wnt/β-catenin signaling activity was evident before sp7:EGFP+ scale papilla had formed (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by live imaging data showing temporal sequence of reporter expression.

claim: After papilla formation, Wnt/β-catenin signaling became polarized toward the posterior scale margin, where it remained throughout scale growth.
source: After papilla formation, Wnt/β-catenin signaling became polarized toward the posterior scale margin, where it remained throughout scale growth.
evidence: This claim is supported by live imaging data showing the spatial pattern of Wnt signaling activity.

claim: lef1 and axin2 were found in skin patches presaging the appearance of scales.
source: In agreement with the 7xTCF:mCherry reporter, lef1 and axin2, as well as nuclear localized β-catenin, were found in skin patches presaging the appearance of scales (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B, pre scale and papilla; Figure 2—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization and immunostaining data.

claim: Expression of lef1 and axin2 subsequently became restricted to a posteriorly biased ring around the circumference of the developing scale.
source: Expression subsequently became restricted to a posteriorly biased ring around the circumference of the developing scale (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B, extension; Figure 2—figure supplement 1E,G,H).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization and immunostaining data showing spatial expression patterns.

claim: axin2 was expressed exclusively in dermal cells and was absent from the epidermis.
source: Although expression dynamics of these Wnt/β-catenin activity markers were broadly similar, axin2 was expressed exclusively in dermal cells and was absent from the epidermis, whereas lef1 was expressed in both dermis and epidermis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data on tissue sections.

claim: lef1 was expressed in both dermis and epidermis.
source: Although expression dynamics of these Wnt/β-catenin activity markers were broadly similar, axin2 was expressed exclusively in dermal cells and was absent from the epidermis, whereas lef1 was expressed in both dermis and epidermis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data on tissue sections.

claim: Early Dkk1 induction prevented patterned expression of lef1 and axin2.
source: As expected for Wnt target genes, early Dkk1 induction prevented patterned expression lef1 and axin2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D, early hs:dkk1).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data from Dkk1-treated fish.

claim: Dkk1-mediated Wnt repression initiated after scales had formed attenuated expression of axin2, but not lef1.
source: However, Dkk1-mediated Wnt repression initiated after scales had formed attenuated expression of axin2, but not lef1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D, late hs:dkk1)
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data comparing early and late Dkk1 treatment.

claim: There is a mechanism independent of Wnt/β-catenin signaling for maintaining lef1 expression during scale outgrowth.
source: However, Dkk1-mediated Wnt repression initiated after scales had formed attenuated expression of axin2, but not lef1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D, late hs:dkk1), suggesting a mechanism independent of Wnt/β-catenin signaling for maintaining lef1 expression during scale outgrowth.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential response of lef1 and axin2 to late Wnt inhibition.

claim: Wnt/β-catenin signaling is necessary for initiation of scale development.
source: Taken together, expression of Wnt/β-catenin target genes prior to papilla appearance and lack of scales in Dkk1 overexpressing fish demonstrates that Wnt/β-catenin signaling is necessary for initiation of scale development.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on multiple lines of experimental evidence presented earlier.

claim: nkt mutants lacked overt indications of scale morphogenesis and sp7:EGFP+ dSFCs in the skin.
source: nkt mutants lacked overt indications of scale morphogenesis and sp7:EGFP+ dSFCs in the skin, in addition to having impaired fin outgrowth (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data from nkt mutant fish.

claim: Wnt/β-catenin activity was patterned into spots in the epidermis of scale-less nkt mutants.
source: Yet, live imaging of sp7:EGFP; 7xTCF:mCherry transgene expression and in situ hybridization against lef1 showed that Wnt/β-catenin activity was patterned into spots in the epidermis of scale-less nkt mutants (Figure 3A–3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by live imaging and in situ hybridization data from nkt mutants.

claim: Wnt/β-catenin targets were initially expressed in scale-appropriate patterns in nkt mutants, yet further rows were not formed and expression domains did not polarize.
source: Wnt/β-catenin targets were initially expressed in scale-appropriate patterns in nkt mutants, yet further rows were not formed and expression domains did not polarize.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and in situ data showing the pattern and extent of Wnt activity in nkt mutants.

claim: Initiation and patterning of Wnt activity in the skin is Eda-independent.
source: These findings indicate that initiation and patterning of Wnt activity in the skin is Eda-independent, whereas later refinement and reiteration of Wnt activity requires Eda signaling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Wnt activity initiates in nkt mutants but does not progress normally.

claim: Later refinement and reiteration of Wnt activity requires Eda signaling.
source: These findings indicate that initiation and patterning of Wnt activity in the skin is Eda-independent, whereas later refinement and reiteration of Wnt activity requires Eda signaling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Wnt activity does not progress normally in nkt mutants.

claim: Wnt signaling alone is not sufficient to induce scales in the absence of Eda.
source: The absence of overt scale development despite initiation of Wnt signaling, also demonstrates that Wnt signaling alone is not sufficient to induce scales in the absence of Eda.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that nkt mutants have Wnt activity but no scales.

claim: eda expression disappeared from epidermal cells above forming scale papillae where edar expression was first detected.
source: Immediately prior to scale formation, eda expression disappeared from epidermal cells above forming scale papillae where edar expression was first detected (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C pre-scale).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data showing complementary expression patterns.

claim: eda was expressed broadly in dSFCs during scale development.
source: Subsequently, eda was expressed broadly in dSFCs whereas edar expression became localized principally to the posterior margin of the scale epidermis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C papilla, extension)
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data showing spatial expression patterns.

claim: edar expression became localized principally to the posterior margin of the scale epidermis.
source: Subsequently, eda was expressed broadly in dSFCs whereas edar expression became localized principally to the posterior margin of the scale epidermis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C papilla, extension)
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data showing spatial expression patterns.

claim: edar expression was strongly attenuated in Dkk1-overexpressing, Wnt/β-catenin inhibited fish.
source: We therefore induced hs:dkk1 following the appearance of initial scales (2R stage) and assayed expression of eda and edar. As predicted, edar expression was strongly attenuated in Dkk1-overexpressing, Wnt/β-catenin inhibited fish, whereas eda expression persisted (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data from Dkk1-treated fish.

claim: eda expression persisted in Dkk1-overexpressing, Wnt/β-catenin inhibited fish.
source: We therefore induced hs:dkk1 following the appearance of initial scales (2R stage) and assayed expression of eda and edar. As predicted, edar expression was strongly attenuated in Dkk1-overexpressing, Wnt/β-catenin inhibited fish, whereas eda expression persisted (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data from Dkk1-treated fish.

claim: Misexpression of either Eda or Edar initiated scale development in fish with normal Wnt/β-catenin signaling.
source: In fish with normal Wnt/β-catenin signaling, misexpression of either Eda or Edar initiated scale development, as revealed by accumulations of sp7:EGFP+ dSFCs in regions where scales do not normally form at these stages (Figure 3G,H, control).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Eda and Edar misexpression experiments.

claim: Misexpression of Eda in either epidermis or dermis initiated ectopic scale development.
source: Misexpression of Eda in either epidermis or dermis initiated ectopic scale development (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B)
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data from Eda misexpression experiments showing ectopic scales.

claim: Edar initiated ectopic scale development only when misexpressed in the epidermis.
source: whereas Edar did so only when misexpressed in the epidermis (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C,D)
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data from Edar misexpression experiments showing tissue-specific effects.

claim: Competence to respond to Eda signaling is unique to epidermis.
source: whereas Edar did so only when misexpressed in the epidermis (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C,D), suggesting that competence to respond to Eda signaling is unique to epidermis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the tissue-specific response to Edar misexpression.

claim: Eda/Edar driven ectopic scale induction was completely blocked in the absence of Wnt/β-catenin signaling.
source: However, Eda/Edar driven ectopic scale induction was completely blocked in the absence of Wnt/β-catenin signaling (Figure 3G–3H, hs:dkk1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data combining Eda/Edar misexpression with Wnt inhibition.

claim: Neither Wnt/β-catenin nor Eda signaling is sufficient to trigger scale development in the absence of the other.
source: Therefore, neither Wnt/β-catenin nor Eda signaling is sufficient to trigger scale development in the absence of the other.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the combined results of Wnt inhibition and Eda/Edar misexpression experiments.

claim: Treatment with pan-Fgf receptor inhibitor BGJ398 led to an immediate and complete arrest of squamation and scale growth without affecting overall somatic growth.
source: This treatment led to an immediate and complete arrest of squamation and scale growth without affecting overall somatic growth of the fish (Figure 4A,B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from BGJ398 treatment showing scale-specific effects.

claim: Fgf signaling is necessary for both scale initiation and outgrowth.
source: This treatment led to an immediate and complete arrest of squamation and scale growth without affecting overall somatic growth of the fish (Figure 4A,B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C), demonstrating that Fgf signaling is necessary for both scale initiation and outgrowth.
evidence: This is an inference based on the complete arrest of both scale initiation and growth upon Fgf inhibition.

claim: fgfr1a, fgfr1b and fgfr2 are expressed in 4R stage skin.
source: To determine which Fgf receptors are involved in scale development, we generated cDNA from 4R stage skin and assayed by RT-PCR the expression of each of the five Fgf receptor genes present in the zebrafish genome. Of these, amplicons for fgfr1a, fgfr1b and fgfr2 were recovered.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data from skin cDNA.

claim: fgfr1a was detected in dSFCs during scale development.
source: While riboprobes against fgfr1b did not yield tissue specific staining, consistent with previous reports (Rohner et al., 2009), fgfr1a was detected in dSFCs and fgfr2 in the epidermal posterior margin during scale development (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data showing spatial expression patterns.

claim: fgfr2 was detected in the epidermal posterior margin during scale development.
source: While riboprobes against fgfr1b did not yield tissue specific staining, consistent with previous reports (Rohner et al., 2009), fgfr1a was detected in dSFCs and fgfr2 in the epidermal posterior margin during scale development (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data showing spatial expression patterns.

claim: hag/+ mutants develop large, disorganized sheets of sp7:EGFP+ dSFCs.
source: We found that hag/+ fish develop large, disorganized sheets of sp7:EGFP+ dSFCs (Figure 4C), a previously overlooked phenotype.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data from hag/+ mutants.

claim: In hag/+ fish with repressed Wnt/β-catenin signaling, neither sheets nor foci of sp7:EGFP+ dSFCs developed in response to fgf8a overexpression.
source: In hag/+ fish with repressed Wnt/β-catenin signaling, neither sheets nor foci of sp7:EGFP+ dSFCs developed in response to fgf8a overexpression (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data combining hag mutation with Wnt inhibition.

claim: hag/+ fish simultaneously homozygous for nkt formed broad sheets of sp7:EGFP+ dSFCs.
source: By contrast, hag/+ fish simultaneously homozygous for nkt—and so lacking Eda but retaining residual Wnt signaling activity (Figure 3A–3D)—formed broad sheets of sp7:EGFP+ dSFCs (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data from double mutant fish.

claim: Fgf-mediated differentiation of dSFCs requires Wnt/β-catenin, but not Eda signaling.
source: Taken together these results show that Fgf-mediated differentiation of dSFCs requires Wnt/β-catenin, but not Eda signaling.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the combined results from hag mutants with Wnt inhibition or Eda loss.

claim: The Wnt-dependence of Fgf signaling is not likely due to modulation of Fgfr gene expression.
source: The Wnt-dependence of Fgf signaling is not likely due to modulation of Fgfr gene expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E,G) but could reflect direct or indirect regulation of other Fgf pathway components yet to be identified.
evidence: This is an inference based on in situ data showing Fgfr expression is maintained in Wnt-inhibited fish.

claim: HH signaling repression did not affect induction or patterning of scales, but did alter scale morphogenesis.
source: These treatments did not affect induction or patterning of scales, but did alter scale morphogenesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from DR-Gli2 and cyclopamine treatments.

claim: Epidermal folding was completely blocked by HH repression.
source: In normal scale development, the epidermis folds around the growing posterior margin of the developing scale (Figure 5A). Strikingly, epidermal folding was completely blocked by HH repression (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data comparing control and HH-repressed fish.

claim: Epidermal morphogenesis during scale development is an active, HH-dependent process and not simply a passive consequence of scale plate growth.
source: These results also demonstrated that epidermal morphogenesis during scale development is an active, HH-dependent process and not simply a passive consequence of scale plate growth, indeed, epidermal folding was completely absent even when underlying scale plates overlapped (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that epidermal folding is blocked even when scale plates are present.

claim: HH signaling began only after papilla morphogenesis.
source: Since HH repression did not interfere with scale induction we predicted that expression of HH pathway genes and signaling activation would appear later in scale morphogenesis. We found that—unlike Wnt/β-catenin, Eda and Fgf signaling—HH signaling began only after papilla morphogenesis (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and in situ data showing the timing of HH pathway activation.

claim: shha was initially expressed in the epidermis overlying the scale papilla and was later restricted to a column of two to three cells at the posterior scale margin.
source: shha was initially expressed in the epidermis overlying the scale papilla and was later restricted to a column of two to three cells at the posterior scale margin (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data showing spatial and temporal expression patterns.

claim: gli2-D:mcherry and hhip were detected in a population of cells beneath the sp7:EGFP+ dSFCs, where expression persisted throughout scale morphogenesis.
source: gli2-D:mcherry and hhip were detected in a population of cells beneath the sp7:EGFP+ dSFCs, where expression persisted throughout scale morphogenesis (Figure 5C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and in situ hybridization data showing HH-responsive cells.

claim: cldnb:EGFP+ epidermal cells invaginated into the underlying dermis in close association with the HH-responding population.
source: To further investigate the requirement for HH signaling in epidermal morphogenesis, we imaged fish doubly transgenic for the epidermal transgene cldnb:EGFP and gli2-D:mCherry throughout scale development. This revealed cldnb:EGFP+ epidermal cells invaginating into the underlying dermis in close association with the HH-responding population (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by live imaging data showing the spatial relationship between invaginating epidermis and HH-responding cells.

claim: Cells at the leading edge of invaginating epidermis revealed hallmarks of active invasive migration including broad lamellipodia and long cellular extensions.
source: Live imaging of cells at the leading edge of invaginating epidermis revealed hallmarks of active invasive migration including broad lamellipodia and long cellular extensions (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by high-resolution imaging data showing cellular morphology.

claim: Shha overexpression in fish transgenic for hs:shha-GFP led to rapid kyphosis, failure to feed and developmental arrest.
source: Unfortunately, Shha overexpression in fish transgenic for hs:shha-GFP led to rapid kyphosis, failure to feed and developmental arrest, precluding analyses of scale morphogenesis (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by observation of phenotypes in hs:shha-GFP fish.

claim: Epidermal cells of hs:shha-GFP fish rapidly moved from the surface of the fish to the glass coverslip.
source: Strikingly, however, epidermal cells of these fish rapidly moved from the surface of the fish to the glass coverslip (Figure 5G).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data from hs:shha-GFP fish.

claim: Cells at the leading edge of the epidermal sheet in hs:shha-GFP fish were cldnb:EGFP+ and displayed numerous long filopodia, consistent with active migration.
source: Cells at the leading edge of this sheet were cldnb:EGFP+ and displayed numerous long filopodia, consistent with active migration.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data showing cellular morphology in hs:shha-GFP fish.

claim: shha, hhip and gli-D:mCherry expression were strongly attenuated in both Wnt-repressed and nkt mutant fish.
source: We therefore assayed expression of HH signaling components while manipulating Wnt/β-catenin and Eda pathways. shha, hhip and gli-D:mCherry expression were strongly attenuated in both Wnt-repressed and nkt mutant fish (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization and imaging data from Wnt-inhibited and nkt mutant fish.

claim: shha expression is regulated by Eda signaling during scale development.
source: Since nkt mutants retain epidermal Wnt signaling activity (Figure 3B) but lack Eda, these data suggest that shha expression is regulated by Eda signaling during scale development.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that shha is lost in nkt mutants despite residual Wnt activity.

claim: One day after scale removal, patterned 7xTCF:mCherry expression revealed Wnt/β-catenin signaling in the epidermis, presaging the appearance of regenerated scales.
source: One day after scale removal, patterned 7xTCF:mCherry expression revealed Wnt/β-catenin signaling in the epidermis, presaging the appearance of regenerated scales (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data from scale regeneration experiments.

claim: Wnt/β-catenin signaling repression during scale regeneration resulted in the regeneration of significantly fewer, slower growing scales as compared to controls.
source: To test the requirement for this activity, we repressed Wnt/β-catenin signaling during scale regeneration by Dkk1 induction. This resulted in the regeneration of significantly fewer, slower growing scales as compared to controls (Figure 6B–6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from scale regeneration experiments with Wnt inhibition.

claim: HH-repression completely blocked epidermal morphogenesis during scale regeneration.
source: Finally, to test the role of HH signaling during regeneration we expressed DR-Gli2 following scale removal. As during scale ontogeny, HH-repression completely blocked epidermal morphogenesis (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data from scale regeneration experiments with HH inhibition.

claim: Wnt/β-catenin and HH signaling play similar roles during scale development and regeneration.
source: Therefore, Wnt/β-catenin and HH signaling play similar roles during scale development and regeneration.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the similar phenotypes observed in developmental and regenerative contexts.

claim: Zebrafish squamation proceeds through an invariant sequence of row and column addition.
source: Our analysis, based on live imaging of individual fish, has revealed the developmental anatomy of squamation and individual scale development. We find that zebrafish squamation proceeds through an invariant sequence of row and column addition (Figure 7A)
evidence: This claim is supported by repeated live imaging data of individual fish.

claim: The squamation sequence documented in zebrafish differs from previous reports based on fixed specimens that inferred a sequential spread of scales from posterior to anterior.
source: this differs from previous reports based on fixed specimens that inferred a sequential spread of scales from posterior to anterior (Sire et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim compares the current findings with previous literature based on different methodology.

claim: The squamation sequence documented in zebrafish resembles that of goldfish (Carassius auratus) and medaka (Oryzias latipes).
source: The sequence we documented resembles that of goldfish (Carassius auratus) and medaka (Oryzias latipes)(Iwamatsu, 2014; Li et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim compares the current findings with published data from other fish species.

claim: The squamation sequence presented potentially represents a conserved, ancestral character of teleosts.
source: Since the lineages leading to zebrafish and medaka are thought to have diverged over 300 million years ago (Near et al., 2012), the squamation sequence presented here potentially represents a conserved, ancestral character of teleosts.
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic considerations and comparative data.

claim: Zebrafish squamation is strikingly reminiscent of the ordered addition of chicken feather and reptile scale anlagen.
source: Zebrafish squamation is also strikingly reminiscent of the ordered addition of chicken feather and reptile scale anlagen, suggesting this mode of patterning is conserved throughout vertebrates (Di-Poï and Milinkovitch, 2016; Jung et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim compares the zebrafish pattern with patterns in other vertebrates from the literature.

claim: Eda and Wnt/β-catenin signaling integrate similarly during fish scale and amniote skin appendage development.
source: We found that Eda and Wnt/β-catenin signaling integrate similarly during fish scale and amniote skin appendage development: (i) Wnt/β-catenin signaling was initiated in the absence of Eda signaling yet pattern refinement and reiteration were Eda-dependent (Figure 3A–D); and (ii) Wnt/β-catenin signaling was necessary for the expression of the Eda receptor, edar (Figure 3F; Houghton et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and comparison with published studies on amniote skin appendages.

claim: While Eda and Fgf signaling are sufficient to drive ectopic differentiation of dSFCs and scale development, these pathways were able to do so only in the presence of functional Wnt/β-catenin signaling.
source: Simultaneous manipulation of multiple signaling activities revealed that while Eda and Fgf signaling are sufficient to drive ectopic differentiation of dSFCs and scale development, these pathways were able to do so only in the presence of functional Wnt/β-catenin signaling.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings from combined pathway manipulations.

claim: There are likely other, as yet unidentified, parallel mechanisms by which Wnt regulates scale development.
source: Since dSFCs do not differentiate in Wnt-inhibited fish with simultaneous upregulation of Eda or Fgf, there are likely other, as yet unidentified, parallel mechanisms by which Wnt regulates scale development (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observation that Eda/Fgf cannot rescue Wnt loss.

claim: Scale development relies on signaling interactions similar to interactions that regulate the patterning and morphogenesis of amniote skin appendages such as hair and feathers.
source: These interactions are again similar to signaling interactions previously described for hair and feather patterning in amniotes (Andl et al., 2002; Houghton et al., 2005; Huh et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2008; Mandler and Neubüser, 2004; Petiot et al., 2003; Sick et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim compares the current findings with published studies on amniote skin appendages.

claim: The findings support a model in which diverse skin appendages of vertebrates arose from a common archetype.
source: These analyses show that scale development relies on signaling interactions similar to interactions that regulate the patterning and morphogenesis of amniote skin appendages such as hair and feathers, and support a model in which diverse skin appendages of vertebrates arose from a common archetype.
evidence: This is an evolutionary inference based on the similarity of developmental mechanisms across vertebrates.

claim: Wnt/β-catenin–Eda dependent HH signaling regulates epidermal morphogenesis during late steps in scale development.
source: During late steps in scale development, we found that Wnt/β-catenin–﻿Eda dependent HH signaling regulates epidermal morphogenesis.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings showing the regulatory hierarchy.

claim: HH signaling is necessary for epidermal morphogenesis during hair and feather development.
source: Since HH signaling is also necessary for epidermal morphogenesis during hair and feather development (McKinnell et al., 2004; St-Jacques et al., 1998)
evidence: This claim cites published studies on amniote skin appendages.

claim: Some functional outputs of skin appendage signaling networks are conserved and anciently evolved.
source: Since HH signaling is also necessary for epidermal morphogenesis during hair and feather development (McKinnell et al., 2004; St-Jacques et al., 1998), it is possible that some functional outputs of skin appendage signaling networks are conserved and anciently evolved.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the conservation of HH function across vertebrates.

claim: There is a previously unappreciated role for invasive migration in epidermal morphogenesis that may be of general relevance to understanding cellular mechanisms underlying skin appendage development and regeneration.
source: In turn, this suggests a previously unappreciated role for invasive migration in epidermal morphogenesis that may be of general relevance to understanding cellular mechanisms underlying skin appendage development and regeneration (Armstrong et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observed cellular behaviors and their potential broader significance.

claim: The analyses of teleost scale developmental genetics using zebrafish are consistent with a single origin of skin patterning mechanisms in ancient fishes that has been conserved in extant vertebrates.
source: Taken together, our analyses of teleost scale developmental genetics using zebrafish are consistent with a single origin of skin patterning mechanisms in ancient fishes that has been conserved in extant vertebrates, even as the final adult morphology of feathers, hairs and scales appear wildly divergent.
evidence: This is an evolutionary inference based on the conservation of developmental mechanisms.

claim: Early tetrapods were endowed with fish-like calcified dermal scales.
source: Importantly, the fossil record indicates that early tetrapods were endowed with fish-like calcified dermal scales (Coates, 1996; Jarvik, 1996)
evidence: This claim cites paleontological evidence from the literature.

claim: There was a progressive loss of calcified matrix in skin appendages over geological time.
source: with a progressive loss of calcified matrix over geological time (Mondéjar-Fernández et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim cites paleontological evidence from the literature.

claim: Skin appendages lost dermal calcified matrix and gained epidermal keratinization ultimately leading to the skin appendages of extant amniotes.
source: In light of conserved developmental regulatory architecture, this suggests a scenario in which skin appendages lost dermal calcified matrix and gained epidermal keratinization ultimately leading to the skin appendages of extant amniotes.
evidence: This is an evolutionary inference based on developmental data and paleontological evidence.

claim: Conservation of molecular mechanisms that regulate skin appendage patterning and early morphogenesis enables the use of zebrafish scale development as a model system for understanding vertebrate skin patterning and morphogenesis.
source: Conservation of molecular mechanisms that regulate skin appendage patterning and early morphogenesis enables the use of zebrafish scale development as a model system for understanding vertebrate skin patterning and morphogenesis with exceptional opportunities for live imaging and forward genetic analysis, complementing existing chicken and mouse models.
evidence: This is a forward-looking statement based on the demonstrated conservation of mechanisms.

claim: sp7 encodes a zinc finger transcription factor that is necessary and sufficient for osteoblast differentiation from committed progenitors.
source: sp7 (formerly osterix) encodes a zinc finger transcription factor that is necessary and sufficient for osteoblast differentiation from committed progenitors (Zhang, 2012).
evidence: This claim cites established knowledge from the literature.

claim: Scales comprise thin, overlapping plates of dentin-like calcified extracellular matrix embedded in the dermis in many extant teleosts.
source: In many extant teleosts, scales comprise thin, overlapping plates of dentin-like calcified extracellular matrix embedded in the dermis (Sire et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim cites established knowledge from the literature.

claim: Fish scales develop relatively late in ontogeny and are distributed across the skin in a tight, hexagonal grid pattern in the adult.
source: Similar to amniote skin appendages, fish scales develop relatively late in ontogeny and are distributed across the skin in a tight, hexagonal grid pattern in the adult.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge and the current observations.

claim: Genetic analyses have identified phenotypes associated with Ectodysplasin-A (Eda) and Fgf mutations in fish scales.
source: Scales have been the object of excellent histological and ultrastructural studies that have characterized developmental anatomy, and genetic analyses that have identified phenotypes associated with Ectosyslasin-A (Eda) and Fgf mutations (Harris et al., 2008; Rohner et al., 2009; Sire et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim cites previous genetic studies from the literature.

claim: Scale morphogenesis begins with the formation of a bi-layered dermal papilla immediately beneath the epidermis.
source: Histological, ultrastructural and fate mapping studies showed that scale morphogenesis begins with the formation of a bi-layered dermal papilla immediately beneath the epidermis (Mongera and Nüsslein-Volhard, 2013; Shimada et al., 2013; Sire et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim cites previous histological and fate-mapping studies.

claim: Squamation initiated from two foci, on the caudal peduncle and on the flank above the ribs.
source: (A,B) Squamation initiated from two foci, on the caudal peduncle (boxed in a), and on the flank above the ribs (red arrowhead in B).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: Squamation initiated in larvae between 8.5 mm and 9.5 mm standard length.
source: (C) Squamation initiated in larvae between 8.5 mm and 9.5 mm standard length (SL; n = 131).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurement data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Squamation was completed over 13 ± 2 days during a period of rapid somatic growth.
source: (D,E) Squamation was completed over 13 ± 2 days during a period of rapid somatic growth.
evidence: This claim is supported by longitudinal measurement data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D,E.

claim: hs:dkk1 larvae developed significantly fewer scales than heat-shocked controls.
source: (C) hs:dkk1 larvae developed significantly fewer scales (n = 21) then heat-shocked controls (n = 13; p<0.0001).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Pectoral fins were significantly shorter in hs:dkk1 larvae than in heat-shocked controls.
source: (D) Pectoral fins were significantly shorter in hs:dkk1 larvae (n = 21) than in heat-shocked controls (n = 13; p<0.0001).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: hs:dkk1 larvae achieved a similar standard length to heat-shocked controls.
source: (E) hs:dkk1 larvae achieved a similar standard length (n = 21) to heat-shocked controls (n = 13; p=0.1).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: lef1 was initially broadly expressed in cuboidal, basal epidermal cells prior to overt scale morphogenesis.
source: (A) lef1 was initially broadly expressed in cuboidal, basal epidermal cells prior to overt scale morphogenesis (pre scale; n = 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: lef1 expression spread to dermal cells of the scale papilla.
source: Subsequently, expression spread to dermal cells of the scale papilla (papilla; n = 6)
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: lef1 expression became restricted to epidermal and dermal cells at the posterior margin during scale extension.
source: before becoming restricted to epidermal and dermal cells at the posterior margin (extension; n = 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: axin2 was expressed in the dermis prior to scale formation.
source: (B) axin2 was expressed in the dermis prior to scale formation (pre scale; n = 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: axin2 expression persisted throughout the dermal papilla and weak expression was detected in epidermal cells.
source: Expression persisted throughout the dermal papilla and weak expression was detected in epidermal cells (papilla; n = 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: axin2 expression ultimately became restricted to dermal cells at the posterior margin and was absent in overlying epidermal cells.
source: axin2 expression ultimately became restricted to dermal cells at the posterior margin (extension) and was absent in overlying epidermal cells (arrowheads; n = 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Induction of hs:dkk1 prior to initial squamation prevented patterned expression of lef1.
source: (C) Induction of hs:dkk1 prior to initial squamation (early hs:dkk1) prevented patterned expression of lef1 (n = 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: hs:dkk1 induction did not affect lef1 expression in scales that had formed prior to induction.
source: hs:dkk1 induction did not affect lef1 expression in scales that had formed prior to induction (late hs:dkk1; n = 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: axin2 expression was abolished from skin when hs:dkk1 was induced prior to squamation.
source: (D) axin2 expression was abolished from skin when hs:dkk1 was induced prior to squamation (early hs:dkk1; n = 8)
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: axin2 expression was abolished from scales that had already formed prior to hs:dkk1 induction.
source: and from scales that had already formed prior to induction (late hs:dkk1; n = 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Nuclear β-catenin was detected in superficial epidermis and deep dermis in pre-scale regions.
source: (F) In pre scale regions, nuclear β-catenin (red) was detected in superficial epidermis (F') as well as deep dermis (F'') (arrows).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Nuclear β-catenin was present in epidermis and in dermal sp7:EGFP+ scale forming cells in scale papilla.
source: (G) In sp7:EGFP+ (green) scale papilla, nuclear β-catenin was present in epidermis (G') and in dermal sp7:EGFP+ scale forming cells (G'', arrows).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Nuclear β-catenin was not detected in epidermis but only in one to two rows of sp7:EGFP+ dermal scale forming cells at the posterior margin in extending scales.
source: (H) In extending scales, nuclear β-catenin was not detected in epidermis (H') but only in one to two rows of sp7:EGFP+ dermal scale forming cells at the posterior margin (H', arrows).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1H.

claim: DMSO-treated fish added more scales than BGJ398-treated fish over a five day treatment period.
source: (A) Scales added over the course of a five day treatment with 0.1% DMSO or 1 µM BGJ398. DMSO-treated fish added more scales then BGJ398-treated fish (p=0.0001).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Scale surface area increased more in DMSO-treated controls than BGJ398-treated fish.
source: (B) Scale surface area increased more in DMSO-treated controls than BGJ398-treated fish (p<0.0001).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Standard length increased similarly in DMSO treated fish and BGJ398-treated fish.
source: (C) Standard length increased similarly in DMSO treated fish and BGJ398-treated fish (p=0.15); n = 8 for all measurements.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: fgfr1a was expressed broadly in epidermis prior to scale formation.
source: (D) fgfr1a was expressed broadly in epidermis prior to scale formation (pre-scale).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: fgfr1a expression shifted to scale forming cells in the dermal papilla.
source: Expression shifted to scale forming cells in the dermal papilla (papilla)
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: fgfr1a expression was maintained in scale forming cells at the posterior margin during scale extension.
source: and was maintained in scale forming cells at the posterior margin (extension).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Wnt repression following scale formation did not affect fgfr1a expression.
source: (E) Wnt repression following scale formation did not affect fgfr1a expression (late hs:dkk1)
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Wnt repression prior to scale formation prevented localized fgfr1a expression.
source: however, repression prior to scale formation prevented localized expression (early hs:dkk1).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Eda mutants (nkt/nkt) did not show patterned fgfr1a expression.
source: Eda mutants (nkt/nkt) did not show patterned fgfr1a expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: fgfr1a expression was maintained in neuromasts of early hs:dkk1 and nkt/nkt fish.
source: Expression was maintained in neuromasts (nm) of early hs:dkk1 and nkt/nkt.
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: fgfr2 was detected broadly in the epidermis prior to scale formation.
source: (F) fgfr2 was also detected broadly in the epidermis prior to scale formation (pre-scale)
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: fgfr2 expression became restricted to the epidermal posterior margin.
source: before become restricted to the epidermal posterior margin (papilla), where it was maintained throughout scale development (extension).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: fgfr2 expression was not affected by Wnt repression after scale formation.
source: (G) Similar to fgfr1a, fgfr2 expression was not affected by Wnt repression after scale formation (late hs:dkk1)
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Patterned fgfr2 expression was blocked by Wnt repression prior to scale formation.
source: although patterned expression was blocked by Wnt repression prior to scale formation (early hs:dkk1)
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Patterned fgfr2 expression was blocked by loss of Eda.
source: and also by loss of Eda (nkt/nkt). n = 6 for all in situ hybridizations.
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Epidermis was folded around the bony scale plates in larvae treated with 1% EtOH throughout squamation.
source: (A) Epidermis (cldnb:EGFP, green) was folded around the bony scale plates (ARS, magenta) in larvae treated with 1% EtOH throughout squamation; n = 8.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 40 µM cyclopamine treatment completely blocked epidermal folding, even when scale plates overlapped.
source: 40 µM cyclopamine treatment completely blocked epidermal folding, even when scale plates overlapped (arrow); n = 8.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Heatshock induction of dominant repressor Gli2 (hs:gli2-DR) strongly attenuated expression of the HH reporter transgene (gli2-D:mCherry).
source: (B,C) Heatshock induction of dominant repressor Gli2 (hs:gli2-DR) strongly attenuated expression of the HH reporter transgene (gli2-D:mCherry; b) and the conserved HH target gene hhip (arrowheads in C).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: shha expression was only detectable in the epidermis following formation of the scale papilla.
source: (D) shha expression was only detectable in the epidermis following formation of the scale papilla (papilla).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: shha expression persisted in two to three rows of cells at the epidermal posterior margin in growing scales.
source: Expression persisted in two to three rows of cells at the epidermal posterior margin in growing scales (extension).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: hhip initiated expression following papilla appearance.
source: (E) The HH target gene, hhip, also initiated expression following papilla appearance (papilla)
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: hhip expression persisted in a population of cells deep to the dermal scale forming cells.
source: and persisted in a population of cells deep to the dermal scale forming cells (SFC).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: shha and hhip expression was not detected in scales following induction of hs:dkk1.
source: (F,G) shha and hhip expression was not detected in scales (arrowheads) following induction of hs:dkk1 (n = 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F,G.

claim: Eda mutants (nkt/nkt) lacked shha and hhip expression.
source: Eda mutants (nkt/nkt) also lacked shha and hhip expression (n = 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F,G.

claim: hs:dkk1 induction attenuated expression of the HH reporter gli2-D:mCherry.
source: (H) hs:dkk1 induction attenuated expression of the HH reporter gli2-D:mCherry; n = 6.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Heat-shocked controls regenerated a significantly higher proportion of scales two days after scale removal than hs:dkk1 fish.
source: (C) Heat-shocked controls regenerated a significantly higher proportion of scales two days after scale removal (2dpp) then hs:dkk1 fish (p=0.0004).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Three days after scale removal, all heat-shocked controls had regenerated their full complement of scales whereas hs:dkk1 fish regenerated significantly fewer scales.
source: Three days after scale removal (three dpp), all heat-shocked controls had regenerated their full complement of scales whereas hs:dkk1 fish regenerated significantly fewer scales (p=0.0007).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Regenerating scales grew more quickly in heat-shocked controls than in hs:dkk1 fish.
source: (D) Regenerating scales grew more quickly in heat-shocked controls than in hs:dkk1 fish (p=0.003).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: In heat-shocked controls, epidermis folded around regenerated scale plates within ten days of scale removal.
source: (E) In heat-shocked controls, epidermis (cldnb:EGFP, green) folded around regenerated scale plates (ARS; magenta) within ten days of scale removal (n = 6)
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: HH repression (hs:gli2-DR) prevented epidermal folding during scale regeneration.
source: whereas HH repression (hs:gli2-DR) prevented epidermal folding (n = 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6E.
